fatal_errors: The proposed simultaneous-reduction mechanism is opposite to the target mechanism, in which Pt, Ir, or Ru reduces first, establishes a lattice, and catalyzes hydrogen-assisted reduction and incorporation of the remaining metals.
The response invents tailored single-source precursors and dynamic process adjustment rather than reconstructing the spray-dried mixed-salt and thermal decomposition-reduction route.
It cannot explain the decisive Pt/Ir/Ru versus Pd and noble-metal-free comparison: nominal reduction synchrony does not account for why Pd fails while Pt, Ir, and Ru enable single-phase alloying.
The cited evidence does not establish synchronized precursor reduction as a general low-temperature formation principle; E2 instead emphasizes stochastic formation and inhibited precursor mobility.
The proposed comparison changes precursor chemistry, monitoring, and processing simultaneously, so a positive result would not isolate reduction synchrony as the causal variable.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad challenge of producing homogeneous, surface-accessible multimetal nanoparticles under moderate reducing conditions, and its predicted single-phase elemental homogeneity overlaps with the reported product. However, it misses the central mechanistic finding. Successful formation did not require all precursors to reduce simultaneously; it depended on sequential noble-metal-first reduction followed by hydrogen dissociation and transfer that enabled reduction and lattice incorporation of Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe. The response also omits the porous 3D nanoframework morphology, the Pt/Ir/Ru-specific enabling behavior, Pd failure, the noble-metal-free control, and Pt–Ru fcc-to-hcp phase tuning. Its experiment is directionally testable but confounded and violates the request to avoid naming the investigated variable and techniques. A decisive target-consistent falsifier would be demonstration that Pt-, Ir-, or Ru-containing systems still form homogeneous single phases when hydrogen dissociation or desorption from the newborn noble-metal surface is suppressed, with no corresponding loss of transition-metal reduction or incorporation.
